utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Mr. Strbac, we had begun to look at some aspects of your prior testimony, but I'd like to clear up a few points. Your work with the civil defence was, in your opinion, intended to protect all citizens, is that correct, irrespective of nationality or ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The appointment of yourself and Mr. Smirko -- I'd like to ask the usher to present Z309.1, please, and I shall try to go through these very quickly mindful of my commitment on time. In front of you, Mr. Strbac, is a report from Anto Bertovic and Sefkija Dzidic dated 12 December 1992 out of Vitez, and this report confirms that you are appointed or nominated for the position by the Vitez HVO and Mr. Sejo, I believe that is a short name for Sulejman, Smirko nominated by the BiH; is this accurate?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I just go through this document because I don't know it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: It is point 2 to which I am referring.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry I really have to read it through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There's no need to read the whole document, Mr. Strbac. Can you now deal with the question which counsel asked?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This report has to do with the 12th of December, 1992, and it has to do with a meeting at which I was not present at all. And item 2, paragraph 1, line 1, where my name is mentioned, I can interpret it only as follows: Since the civil defence, as a part of the defence system, was housed in the secretariat for defence, I -- my guess is that my name is mentioned simply as the name of a person who was the chief of the municipal staff of the civil defence, and the civil defence is part of the defence system so that it is a part of the whole concept of the development of plans of defence in the municipality of Vitez. It doesn't say that the HVO appointed me. It was simply a meeting of the representatives of the Croat Defence Council and the BH army. And when they speak about the plans for the municipality of Vitez, then it is logical for the civil defence, as a part of the defence system, being mentioned within this context.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: It is clear, it is not, from this document that there appears to be a separateness, there is HVO and BiH already at that point and the separateness has made its way on to official documents; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't comment on that document, I repeat, because I was not at that meeting and it has nothing to do with my competencies.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Moving on. Your comments about Mr. Smirko's departure from the position as commander of the civil defence, when, in fact, was he appointed originally, if you know?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean. Could you please clarify?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: When did he become commander of the civil defence?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometime towards the end of 1991 or early 1992. I do not remember exactly. But it is at that time, roughly, end of 1991 and beginning of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And when did he leave?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Sulejman Smirko did not leave. We cannot say that he withdrew either. I said that step by step, gradually, in a way, the Bosniak component began to distance itself and Mr. Smirko left Vitez. I wouldn't know the date, but I know that the open conflict of the 16th of April was well on the way. So it could have been in May or perhaps June 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: In Aleksovski you were asked: Q What happened such that he stopped working there? A When the conflict started in April of 1993 between the HVO and the then Territorial Defence or, as they call it, the army of the BH, Mr. Smirko did not see fit -- and I must say that we didn't see fit either -- fit for him to continue in this position. And in this period of the month of April, he was still in Vitez. He continued to live in his apartment where I visited him on several occasions. We had a couple of conversations in that regard, and he personally considered that it would not be right for him to continue in this position. So I took over as commander of the civilian protection staff. And I must say on this occasion, that after about a month, after the start of the conflict, at his personal request, and with our assistance, he moved to the territory of Zenica municipality. And I don't know if I should add this, even though I personally was trying to convince him to stay, he said that he wanted to go where all his people went. It is a fact, is it not, that this is a post-Ahmici departure, as a matter of fact. A departure after the greatest number of villages cited in -- I'm sorry, you would not know necessarily all the villages, but after the village attacks in the Lasva Valley that he left after those attacks; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can agree only with that part of the statement where I indicated reasons for Mr. Smirko's departure. As for attacks, you were not specific enough. Who attacked whom? What do you think? If you meant attacks by the Bosniaks, Muslims, on our villages, then I can agree.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Was it also a factor in his decision, if he shared this with you, that as someone who was not a member of the HVO government and having held a position integral to the Vitez municipal works, that he could not remain opposing the power which had taken over the functions of Vitez municipality? Did he tell you that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but I really did not understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: He was not a member of the HVO, was he? He was not part of the HVO government, was he?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Well ...

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: At that point in time, you would concede that the HVO was --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Smirko was a member, that is, the commander, of the municipal staff of the civil defence in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I don't know whether the Court would ask or would care to have it in front of itself again, but we had presented Z2298 in the course of earlier testimony which are the Narodni Lists. The only point I wanted to make is that the Narodni Lists governing Herceg-Bosna legislation do include the provisions for civil defence which governed at that time. If the Court does not wish to spend time, I won't. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You were also in charge, were you not, of responses to fires that occurred in Vitez municipality, is that correct, making sure that fires were extinguished so as not to endanger persons or property?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If we are talking about the time when combat operations were taking place, yes, we were in charge, but without endangering men or, rather, firemen, without putting their lives at risk when extinguishing fires.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: This was one of your functions as of the period from the 16th of April to approximately the 21st of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't my function. That is the task of the civil defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Of which you were the head?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The chief, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Would you please describe as briefly but as thoroughly as possible the efforts that were made under your leadership to extinguish the fires which were visible, basically, from the Ahmici village on the 16th up till, minimally, the 20th in Gacice?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As regards Ahmici, in that period of time -- there are two things: The first and fundamental thing is that when the conflict began, when the attack of the army, when they began to attack the territory of the municipality of Vitez, we lost all the equipment of the voluntary fire brigade in Vitez, which is still located in the town of Vitez called Mahala. This is one detail. The second detail. When you asked me about the fire extinction in the inhabited places, I said that, yes, true, the task of the civil defence is to salvage the property and save human lives under such circumstances due to the emergence of fires, without, however, putting at risk the lives of firemen taking part in such an action. As regards Ahmici, I, as the chief, while the fighting was going on, with a couple of my assistants, I was accommodated on the staircase of the post office building in Vitez. We heard detonations around us and gunfire, so I did not even think I had to undertake anything because fighting was going on. Thus, I have said, the equipment, it stayed up there, and all we had at our disposal was one vehicle at the Impregnacija company. The vehicle was made in 1963, and I'm not sure it could really leave the compound or the factory, let alone go to any action. As regards Gacice, from that direction, likewise, while the fighting was going on, I could not undertake anything with those few firemen who had been assigned to my unit. If we were to carry out a proper action, we needed the necessary prerequisites. As for Ahmici, we could do something only after the fighting ended, but that was only two or three days later. We came out into the field but everything had already burned down, so there was no need for us to undertake any extinction of fire. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: This Court has heard considerable evidence that the attacks on Ahmici and the other villages occurred very early in the morning while people were asleep, highly suggestive of pre-planning. In the event there is a finding of pre-planning, can you please tell us what pre-planned fire prevention methodology should have been in place, if you can?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To begin with, and I go back to that thesis, I cannot agree with the first part of your statement that the attack on Ahmici had begun. I cannot agree with that. It is a fact that the reverse took place, that all the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Strbac, you're not here to argue the point. We've heard much evidence about this matter. What you're being asked is what planning should there have been for the fire services before these events?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before these events, we had our plans of protection and rescue. As for the fire prevention in inhabited places, every citizen was duty-bound to have a fire extinguisher at home, and our task was to put up fire extinguishers in those places where there was a water supply network.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The use of incendiary bullets was documented in the village of Gacice. Are you suggesting that a resident of a house whose house is set on fire by an incendiary bullet is obligated under your law to put it out with a fire extinguisher situated at home?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know what the houses were torched with. I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Z450.1, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: This document, Mr. Strbac, is dated 8 February 1993. It is a programme of work on the development of a defence plan for the municipality, municipal bodies, enterprises and other legal entities. It bears the stamp of the Croatian Defence Council in Vitez. And the sections, because it is lengthy, I shall point out the sections to which I would ask your comment. In particular, there is on the second page of the document in English, let me see if it matches up, but it would be above the sections listing Marjan Skopljak, Marko Knezevic, Cerkez, et cetera, it talks about: "The procedure for the development of a defence plan shall be preceded by the development of a working programme," that's condition number 1, and "the drawing up of the estimate of the military-political, economic and other conditions in the event of aggression of other possible conflicts. The defence office shall prepare and issue --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you slow down please because we do not have it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Would it help to put the Croatian on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: "The Defence office shall prepare of military-political conditions. The following shall be responsible for the execution of the above task," in other words everything I have just mentioned. That lists: "1) Marjan Skopljak; 2) Marko Knezevic; 3) Mario Cerkez; and 4) Anto Bertovic." At the bottom of the page in English, comment on the outline. It indicates that: "All bodies responsible for defence preparations shall be obligated to define specific measures of readiness in accordance with the outline of the Plan on Measures of Readiness of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. The Defence Office shall be responsible for the development of the appropriate annexes and necessary legal instruments," et cetera. Turning the page, there is a specific mention of yourself. It lists all bodies responsible for, and then "commander Anto Bertovic," et cetera, and "head of the civilian protection, Dragan Strbac, shall organise the call-up service for the peoples or civilians protection units." Going down a ways, just above Roman numeral IV, it says, "The persons responsible for all these tasks shall be department heads and directors of enterprises and other legal entities." Other legal entities, Mr. Strbac, yes or no, would include the military, would it not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm trying to follow you. But a moment ago I simply couldn't follow you. I couldn't find where that was written.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Above Roman numeral IV, the persons responsible, et cetera, et cetera, and other legal entities. "Other legal entities" includes the military, does it not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But need not.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Number V, Roman V, use of civilian protection. "All bodies responsible for defence preparations and legal entities in the municipality shall develop a method of organising and executing personal and collective protection, measures of protection, and rescue, and the use of units and representatives of civilian protection. The Civilian Protection Municipal Staff manages all activities regarding the drafting of documents on the deployment of civilian population." That would be you, would it not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is related to the employment of the civil defence. Yes, these are the terms of reference, the competencies.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you. The disciplinary possibilities under the laws of Herceg-Bosna, in your opinion, were you able to impose disciplinary action against, for example, a Muslim person who did not consider himself subject to the laws of Herceg-Bosna but rather to the laws of the legitimate government of Bosnia-Herzegovina? What would you do in such a situation?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not apply the laws of Herceg-Bosna. At the time, the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna, we used the law on all national defence, the federal and the republican which we had taken over. And as for disciplinary measures, disciplinary measures cannot be divided on ethnic grounds. They can be pronounced on the grounds of non-compliance with one's duties. And the civil defence, I am referring to all the members of the civil defence, regardless of their ethnic origin, ethnic or religious.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Are you suggesting, then, that a person, a Muslim person, for example, who was subject to a call-up under the laws of Herceg-Bosna and did not comply because, for example, he or she might be pitted against a fellow Muslim, what would happen in that situation? Please give us your reading of what your obligation would be to enforce what you see to be an obligation.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd rather not comment on mobilisation because I was not responsible for it. We can discuss the terms of reference of the civil defence and the mobilisation was under the jurisdiction of the municipal defence office.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: A quick look at Z451.1, please. This document dated 9 February 1993, one day after the document we just looked at in some detail, is the decision signed by Ivan Santic as president of the Vitez HVO and it appoints an operative body for the defence of Vitez municipality. Mario Cerkez's name appears as the second person, the brigade commander, and your name appears as the sixth name, head of the civilian population. This is prior in time to the departure of Mr. Smirko, as I understand your testimony. There is no reference to Mr. Smirko a Muslim here; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But why is it so? Mr. Sulejman Smirko is a volunteer. Yesterday, when we discussed the composition of the municipal staff and we said that there was the commander, the chief, and members, Mr. Sulejman Smirko commanded the municipal staff of the civil defence as a volunteer. And this decision, when referring to me, my name figures here because I'm a professional. That is, I am a full-time employee in the defence secretariat, that is, the office for national defence -- no, the defence office in Vitez as a professional, and I am here as a professional individual. I am talking about myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Was Mr. Smirko the only Muslim in the defence office at a high level, volunteer or otherwise?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean high level? What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: High-ranking capacity.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the defence office, the only official is the gentleman who is the chief of the defence office who was the only one who is authorised to sign everything, and that is Mr. Marijan Skopljak. There could be Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. nobody else except and unless he then empowered somebody else.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The relationship between work units which were outside of the immediate downtown area of Vitez, let's say, on the front or other areas of combat, the relationship between the commander of the armed units and the civilian defence, I would like to discuss and get your opinion, please, about that relationship. First, my question is: Were work units that you discussed yesterday also used to support military units?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday, I talked about civil defence units and work units. When I explained what general-purpose civil defence units were, I said that often, the general population called them "work platoons". In order to answer your question, could you please tell me exactly which work units you are referring to because of the terminology involved? Are you referring to the work units, the work platoons that were used for the needs of the armed forces or are you referring to general-purpose work units of the civil defence?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I suppose both, but in particular, the question is about those work units which were taken out to combat areas during time of combat. Were those civilian defence assigned work units turned over to the military? Were they supporting military activity? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as work platoons that were used for the armed forces are concerned, I cannot talk about those that were established until the 24th of January, 1993 because I was not in charge of such platoons.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "Before", sorry, interpreter's mistake.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Persons who were not able to be conscripted for whatever reasons by the armed forces, I presume by the HVO, those persons were some of the persons who were subject to being called up to the work units; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All who were able, that is to say, up to the age of 60 were duty-bound after general mobilisation was declared to report to the defence office in charge, and when speaking of such persons, they would be assigned to civil defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: From the end of January 1993 until, let us say, July 1993, including, of course, the period of April, the attack period, were Muslims considered persons who were able to be conscripted by the armed forces, in your opinion, as head of the civil defence office?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All citizens are duty-bound to give their contribution to the defence of the area that they are in, irrespective of their ethnic or religious affiliation and in every way at that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: In Aleksovski, the attorney for Mr. Aleksovski asked you: Q Does it mean that these work units could also be used to support the military units? A As I said, anything that had to do with the defence and continuation of life there, so they could do that as well. The relationship of your work to the Vitez Brigade, can you comment on that, please?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Vitez Brigade, from its establishment onwards, dealt with military matters exclusively, whereas the civil defence, at least to the extent to which it could operate at the time, dealt in civilian defence matters. As far as concerted action is concerned, I don't see any that was there, but of course we did cooperate when there were killings on either side of the front line. Then, our recovery units had to go out and collect the dead and do with them what I discussed yesterday, that is to say, give them a proper burial and everything else that was involved.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And are you suggesting or are you telling us that there was no oversight or otherwise monitoring by the brigade of any of the activities that you performed in the course of your official functions?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The authority of the Vitez Brigade or any other military unit for that matter is not to supervise and monitor the work of the civil defence, it is exclusively under the authority of the civilian government of Vitez, the municipality of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And you do not recall ever having to report to them or keeping them apprised of any particular matters; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As regards whether I had to or not, I did not have to. But if a report was being made, then it was done only by way of information if something was important for a given institution, but I didn't have to. I could only provide by way of information a report of mine, but I was not duty-bound to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Z886.1, please. This is a document dated 5 May 1993, military secret signed by an individual named Slavko Maric. Who is Slavko Maric, do you know?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Apparently the operations or duty officer of the Vitez Brigade -- I'm sorry, to the Vitez Brigade. And the -- it refers to a matter concerning apparently one of your functions and the second paragraph, "At 2230 hours, the duty operative officer, Dragan Strbac, informed us that he could not accommodate the Muslim refugees in the OS elementary school because a group of these refugees did not want to return to Vitez from Divjak, by the UN, for reasons of personal security," et cetera, et cetera. Is this a common practice that you can tell us about, to keep each other informed?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to go back to this document. I do not recall having carried out this activity at all or having been in charge of it. This is the first time I see this document. I don't know why my name is here because I do not remember at all being involved in the accommodation of these Bosniak Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You suggested yesterday that you were somewhat physically bound to Vitez that it was difficult to get around. Can you explain how a person in your position would not be able to get out to see the areas where work platoons or work units were sent, to supervise and make sure thing were okay?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When saying that movement is restricted, that is not to say that it was not at all possible. It was not desirable because we all risked our personal security if we moved about further. I am not referring only to the Lasva River Valley but to the entire of Vitez. This took place seldom, as I said, on one's own responsibility and risk. On the other hand, when speaking of work platoons or rather general-purpose civil defence units, I had commanders of these units. I went to see them when I could and when I had the time to do so to see what they were doing, to see whether they were acting upon instructions of the municipal staff of the civil defence. As regards the activity of work platoons that were carrying out activities for the needs of the armed forces, I did not tour them. As I said, at that time, I was not in charge of seeing what they were doing and in which way.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You were asked in Aleksovski: Q ... By the nature of your job, you sometimes would go to the front lines; is that correct? A Yes. Q During your visits to the front lines and your conversations with soldiers who were defending this area, did you ever see any soldier wearing the HV, the Croatian army insignia? I'm asking not about the insignia but about you being on the front lines. A My duties and my job called for constant moving around. I told you that this was risky, but I had to take that risk, so I was constantly on the move. I never saw, I never heard of anybody with the HV insignia. I would like to ask you -- excuse me. I'm terribly sorry about my voice. I want to be sure I understand your position. What was the legal justification for compelling Muslims to serve in work units that might be involved in actions against the ABiH? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Somers, you asked questions about soldiers wearing HV insignia or, rather, you recited passages.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I did, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But you didn't get a specific response from the witness. Did you not want a response?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Unless it differs radically, Your Honour, from his previous testimony, I'm happy to ask:

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Do you stand by your comment that you never saw any HV insignia, or have you reconsidered your position?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never saw HV insignia, not HVO insignia. As for the statement, the claim that we were compelling Muslims, that particular word, I cannot agree with that at all. I repeat once again that all able-bodied men, citizens of Vitez, men up to the age of 60 and women up to the age of 55, were duty-bound to make themselves available to the institutions in charge of defending our area. So there is no compulsion involved. This is an obligation prescribed by law.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: This Court has heard testimony of a woman named [redacted] whose husband, after being released from Kaonik, was sent back to his then home in Vitez for daily, as it were, forceful assignments on the front lines digging trenches. That type of activity was under your jurisdiction, was it not? He was a civilian; he was forced to dig at Loncari and various places. Can you comment on that, please?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Specifically, I said that all work platoons, that is to say, general purpose units of the civil defence and work platoons that were established for the needs of the armed forces, were under my jurisdiction, as far as I can remember, from the 24th of January 1994. Until then I was in charge only of civil defence units, not of work platoons that were established for the needs of the armed forces. When speaking about work platoons that were established for the needs of the armed forces, my comment would be that they were set up in keeping with the republican and federal legislation that was in force at the time and that regulated this particular area. These regulations were taken over both from republican and/or federal levels.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Somers, I should merely like to -- this could be regarded as a gentleman's agreement. I'd like to remind you of the cross-examination with regard to the examination-in-chief in terms of the time. I think this is this agreement. You've got to comply with it, to heed it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You're right, Your Honour. I was hoping for shorter answers. I have about three more points and then I'll get back into the range of keeping my word. I'm terribly sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I would like to ask you a couple of matters which I think are critical for the Court and then we shall terminate. A question was asked of you by Mr. Niemann, the Prosecutor: Q So under the control of the HVO, were there any particular work units over which you had responsibility which were made up of purely Muslim people? Can you answer that now quickly?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already gave an answer to that. As regards the period until the 24th of January, 1994, I did not have any jurisdiction over any work platoon that consisted of Muslims only. Whether there were any such units until then, I cannot go into that at all. I did have jurisdiction over general purpose civil defence units that consisted of Croats and Serbs and Muslims and Romanie, et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your response to that question indicated that: A ... It was a work unit from town, mostly composed of conscripts. Discussing the makeup of units, A ... They were conscripts of a work responsibility or civilian protection. They were not civilians. Because if he is a recruit, a conscript, once he has been given his war assignments, that individual becomes either a conscript of civilian protection units or the armed forces. So he would take up his work duties and therefore we did not have civilians. In other words, there really is no such thing as a civilian once they are in combat areas; that is correct, is it not? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Again, I have to go back to this. I was not in charge only from the 24th -- I mean, not only these work units from town but also two other work units, I had them as Sofa 1 and Sofa 2 in my files. And they consisted exclusively of persons of Romany ethnic background. But as I said yesterday, according to the decision of the municipal government of the HVO of Vitez, the civil defence took over all those work platoons.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You were asked: Q ... a military commander would say, "What I would like is for say a trench to be dug here," and once he indicated where it was to be located, it was then a matter for the commander of the unit to carry out that task ... A So, the task was, yes, the defence department and civilian protection department in which I worked, I assisted in sending people to carry out their assignments; and when they would get to the particular locality where they were to perform their assignments, then those people would be taken over by the commander of the front line, and he would cooperate with the commander of the front line to see what activities were to be done. I would like to ask you, getting to the very last points, about your reactions and actions to the detention centres in Vitez. Can you tell us, please, from your office which was essentially in Vitez town, what did you observe about the activity in the cinema, hotel, in the SDK, in the chess club? What did you observe about the activity related to detainees there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until the 16th of April, I said that the office of the civil defence of the municipal government was housed in the municipality building. The first five or six days, because the municipality of Vitez was under heavy shelling, we -- I mean, I and a few of my assistants -- stayed at the staircase of the PTT building of the municipality. And as far as I can remember, five or six days later we transferred to the town library building. As regards the events in the buildings that you referred to, I did not go to such places. I was too busy with my own affairs. As I said, during these first five or six days, I didn't even go home at all. I spent all my time there trying to organise certain matters related to civil defence. Naturally, I went to the field every now and then when I had to, at the time. So I did not have to go to these -- I don't remember how you put it, but those few places that you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You were asked by Mr. Niemann: Q During the period of time in 1993 when you were in Vitez, there were members of the Bosniak population who were being held in detention in Vitez, weren't there, from time to time? Were you aware of that? A No, I'm not aware of that. Q So you never heard of a situation where civilian Bosniak people were rounded up and held in detention centres in Vitez in the whole period of the time you were there? A I'm not acquainted with that. I didn't hear of anything like that. I don't know what period you have in mind. Are you referring to the entire period of 1993? Q No, the first half of 1993, from January to July of 1993. You never heard of anyone being held in detention centres in Vitez, in cinema complexes or chess clubs? A I'm not acquainted with this. Let me just tell you one thing ... And then you went on discuss you not going home for I believe you said 15 days, in this version. Q So if I was to ask you, did you from time to time go to detention centres in order to obtain Bosniak workers to go to the front line and dig trenches, then your answer would be no, I take it." A In Vitez, as far as I know, there were no detention centres in Vitez. So I did not have the possibility of going there. Is that still your evidence?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Detention centres, I claim until the present day, did not exist. If they did exist, they were not detention centres. These were places where one could take shelter for the purpose of one's own safety, of every individual. As you know yourself, the war had started. War operations were well under way, and there are always irresponsible individuals. So I still claim that these were not prisons or detention centres; these were places where persons could seek shelter for their own personal safety. I also still abide by the assertion that I had no need to appear in such places. As for this question that I was taking someone away, as I said then, I claim until the present day, I never took anyone anywhere. If we called up someone to serve in the civil defence, that was within the relevant legislation, within the regulations that were then prescribed by the relevant legislation.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: No further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I shall be very brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Strbac, you have seen a document, Z886.1, it was shown to you by the Prosecutor. Part of this document says that you were the operations officer on duty and you gave your answer.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you something else. In this document, it says in reference to a group of persons of Muslim ethnicity that Croat families in Rijeka accommodated about 150 persons in their own homes. Is this an isolated case, or to the best of your knowledge, were there several examples of this nature at the time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One could find such examples everywhere. When speaking of war in our territory, it is true it was the way it was. But you have to understand that we all lived together, next to one another, and regardless of the conflict that broke out, persons were still linked as neighbours, as friends, and there were such cases everywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. You were also shown document Z450.1 which is the programme of work for elaborating the defence plan for the municipality. Tell me, Mr. Strbac, this programme for your plan of work, was this the legal obligation of all municipalities in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina in case of a threat of war?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly. This had to be done, and the way in which this would be carried out was regulated by bylaws in terms of the regulations that were then in force.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were also asked by the Prosecutor about a Muslim person with the surname of Neslanovic. Do you know such a person who was Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. from the territory of the municipality of Vitez?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The surname Neslanovic does exist in the municipality of Vitez; however, I don't know that particular person at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Strbac, the village of Loncari has also been mentioned. Is that village in the territory of the municipality of Busovaca or Vitez?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The village of Loncari is in the territory of the municipality of Busovaca, not the municipality of Vitez. When we look at the communication between Vitez and Kaonik, it is on the left-hand side, that is to say that it is above the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Also a question was put to you in relation to an action that was planned in advance for an attack against the Muslim villages in the territory of the municipality of Vitez. I have another question for you. As a member of the government, the civilian government of the HVO of Vitez, and as a member of the defence department of the municipality of Vitez, did you have any knowledge about the existence of a plan that had been previously prepared before the 16th of April, 1993, in order to attack Muslim villages in the territory of the municipality of Vitez?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a small correction. I was not a member of the defence department. I was an employee there. I am not aware of any such plan at all or was I ever in contact with such documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: My last question, Mr. Strbac: My colleague, the Prosecutor, in her initial questions asked you whether you talked to the representatives of the Defence in this case and in other cases and you said yes, and that you testified in Defence cases. That is undeniable, of course. I'm going to ask you something else: Did any investigator or official from the Office of the Prosecutor of this Tribunal approach you and ask you to make a statement?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the Office of the Prosecutor? No, no, not me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Strbac, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give it. You are now free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, before we move to our next witness, this is Mr. Zarko Krizanovic, can I please submit an argument. I did not want to interrupt my learned colleague once she asked her questions but I need to point out one thing. In framing their questions, the Prosecution seems to be implying a theory which is presented as a fait accompli, and this is an issue that should be an issue that has to be proved here. I think that these questions should not be framed in this way, implying certain facts, because these are the facts that have to be proved here and we would like to ask that these questions not be asked in such a manner. Because if it is implied that what they are trying to prove is a fact, then obviously we are not given an opportunity to counter this with our own arguments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Which questions have you in mind, Mr. Mikulicic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have in mind the question by Ms. Somers which was asked of the witness this morning when she said that "the previously-planned attack on the Muslim villages in Ahmici," it was implied that this was a pre-planned operation and then only then and in that light, the question was asked. When the witness then tried to say that he did not agree with the fact that this was a pre-planned attack on Muslim villages, he was not allowed to expand on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I didn't allow him because we have spent a year and a half on this case. We know the issues. We know the evidence which is going to be given. The question was: What preparation should have been made by the fire services? That was the essence of the question. It was not an invitation to debate the pros and cons of the attack on Ahmici. I know you put in issue that it was a pre-planned and organised attack. It's very much at the forefront of our minds. Of course in some courts, you have to be careful to ensure that questions are not framed in such a way that the witness is taken advantage of or it is suggested that something is proved which it is not. But this Tribunal is different to this extent: The Court consists of professional Judges. We are more than alive to what is in issue and what is not, particularly in this case, if I may say so, with respect. So no unfairness is caused to the witness. If it is, then, of course, the question can be rephrased. I have no doubt that the Prosecution are only too well aware that the issue of whether there was the attack on Ahmici was pre-planned or not is a live issue. Yes, can we have the next witness please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, take the affirmation if you would.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat, Mr. Krizanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Krizanovic.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: On behalf of Mr. Cerkez's Defence, I will ask you some questions in support of your statement, and will you please answer those questions to the best of your recollection. Also, I would like to ask you when you answer my questions, you pause before you give an answer so that we would enable the interpreters to interpret first my questions, then your answers. For the record, Mr. Krizanovic, will you please state your full name, your date and place of birth?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Zarko Krizanovic. I was born on 3 April 1975 in Travnik. I reside in the village of Gacice, number 44, in the Vitez municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You are a Croat by ethnic background and your religion is Roman Catholic?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You are a citizen of BiH, but you also have a citizenship of the Republic of Croatia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You are married?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am married and I have two small children.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You are currently a police officer and you work in the MUP of the Central Bosnia County; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You completed elementary school in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And following that, the electrotechnical secondary school in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What year did you graduate from your secondary school?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: In April 1992. This was an early graduation due to the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In April of 1992 when, due to the war, the school year was interrupted, you were actually 17?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krizanovic, you said that you reside the in the village of Gacice?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what kind of village it is in terms of ethnic composition?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: It is mixed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What does that mean? Which ethnic groups are represented there?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Croat and Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Are Muslim and Croat houses grouped together or are they mixed?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: The village is separated by a road. In the lower part of the village below the road, it's mixed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, the village is divided into two parts, so to speak, by the road that passes through it?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The upper part of the village is almost exclusively inhabited by Muslims?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, by Muslims, but there are some Croats on the other side of the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And the lower part of the village, Croat and Muslims live mixed?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The village of Gacice is right by the SPS factory?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The fence of the SPS is about 150 metres from my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And your father worked for the SPS; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Even though at that time, you were still under age, you can perhaps still tell us whether before 1993, that is, in the latter part of 1992, there was some friction between the Muslims and Croats in the village of Gacice?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Very little. There was some.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: There is a cultural hall in the village; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, what is its role?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: It's a hall that was built by everybody together, but the access to this hall before the war, before the elections, for the most part, the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. access to it had mostly Muslims because they were mostly in the communist party. That was until the first half of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that the Croat part of the village, that the Croats did not have access to this cultural hall?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: They had access with the permission of a person who had the key who was from the other side, that is, he was a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In 1991, you were -- you were still going to school, but the war had broken out in the neighbouring republics of Slovenia and Croatia, especially in 1992. Do you know whether some people from your area, from the surrounding villages, do you know whether they went to fight in Croatia against the JNA?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Were these only people of Croat ethnic background or were there some Muslims around them?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: There were some Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can you give us an example, perhaps, of a Muslim from your village who went to such a mission to defend Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was Sedzad Subasic. He was a neighbour of mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: When the war broke out in Bosnia-Herzegovina, did he come back from Croatia to Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know, were there some others who had also gone to Croatia come back to Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: They probably did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Specifically, the gentleman you mentioned, Sedzad Subasic, who was your neighbour, you must have seen him when he came back. Did he bring any military equipment with him?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: He brought an HOS uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: How about weapons?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Probably. I didn't see it though.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: After 8 April 1992 when the HVO was formed, were Muslims in your village also members of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Not my neighbours, but there were Muslims in the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know someone who you know was a member of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Adis Cosic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Where is this man from?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: He is from Krizancevo Selo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krizanovic, we said that the war moved from the neighbouring Croatia to the territory of your republic, Bosnia-Herzegovina. The JNA had attacked, and in early 1992, what did the village where you lived do in relation to that?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: The village guards were formed on peoples' own initiative because proximity of the SPS and law and order fell apart. There were lootings and people started being afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the presence SPS near your village. We have heard a lot of evidence about the SPS. It was a factory that worked for the former JNA doing military production.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: After the JNA left this territory, was there fear that the JNA air force might bomb this factory?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date, but it must have been in April, or perhaps in early May, there was the first bombing of the factory.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: This, in a way, demonstrated that the formation of this village guard was fully justified.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You mentioned as one of the reasons for the formation of these village guards the rise of the crime rate in the area, and that corresponded to the fact that the rule of law had broken down. Did refugees also appear from the north-western territories of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Specifically in your village, did a number of refugees arrive, and were they placed in various houses?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Were these people of Croat or Muslim ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: At first it was all Muslims from Western Bosnia and Eastern Bosnia, that is, until the fall of Jajce.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Is it true that they predominantly moved into the houses in the upper part of the village where, for the most part, Muslims resided?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: There were some around my house too, but for the most part they were in the upper part of the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You said that the village itself organised these village guards. Were these guards from the beginning monoethnic, or were they mixed in the beginning, consisting of both Muslims and Croats?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: At first they were joint, that is, they were mixed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What weapons did they have available to them?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Until the takeover of the barracks in Slimena, for the most part these were hunting weapons and some pistols.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krizanovic, I know that in early 1992 you were only 17 years old, you were practically a child, but can you remember whether there were enough weapons for every member of the village guards or not?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In other words, there were more members of the village guards than pieces of weaponry.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Many more.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: How was it organised?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: When you arrived to your shift, you would be given some weapon, a rifle or something; and then when you were off a shift, you'd turn it over to someone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Was there somebody who was the commander of this village guard?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: How would somebody from the village become commander of the village guard?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it would simply be that the villagers themselves would designate one person and say, "You will be the commander."

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And then if this person would agree, then he would become the commander.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And if he would not agree?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: He would not become the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You were 17 at the time. Did you ever take part in the village guards at that time?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Occasionally, but I was not duty-bound to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You mentioned a facility called Slimena. We have heard a lot of evidence about this facility. But I will just remind you that that was the former JNA barracks; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: From this barracks, after the pullout of the JNA, the weapons were distributed.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And your village was allotted some of those weapons.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What type of weapons did you get?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: There were real rifles; there were automatic rifles, semi-automatic rifles. There were some that had been partially burned, so people tried to repair those.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Was there a system to this distribution, or were the weapons evenly distributed in the village? Let me rephrase the question. Perhaps I wasn't quite clear. Were the weapons distributed evenly to both Croats and Muslims or not?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: They were distributing to their own people, and our own people were distributing to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You said that at first, the village guards were mixed but then people separated. And then in the Croat part of the village, Croats kept these watches; in the Muslim part, the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can you remember, when did this division take place along ethnic lines?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: After the takeover of the Slimena barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you recall when the first more serious incident took place in your village in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can you please briefly describe this incident to us.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: There was this facility M-1 in the SPS. Near this facility, there were anti-aircraft guns deployed. The crew was mixed; it consisted of both Croats and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. I'll interrupt you. The guns you just mentioned were for protection of the SPS facilities; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: These guns were, in fact, the property of the SPS, according to the law.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Go on.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: In October 1992, there were some incidents. I don't know exactly what happened, but I know that Muslims came down - this was near my house - and they surrounded the guns. Our men - I knew one of those who was part of the crew - they disarmed them and sent them home.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: If I understand you well, what you just told us, the crews of these anti-aircraft guns, the Muslim citizens took over control and they drove away those crew members who were of Croat ethnic background.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Then what happened with these guns?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. But I heard that they were taken to Old Vitez, which was maybe 400 or 500 metres away from the original placement of these guns.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Is that the part of Vitez also known as Mahala?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Are you certain, in other words, did you see at some point that those guns were no longer in places where they had originally been put?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: But you never saw when they were taken away.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I understand. And that was the reason why this incident took place in the village.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What happened then? What was this incident all about?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: I was at home, and several rounds of fire were fired. I don't know whether anybody was injured or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So you just heard some shooting in the village.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: After that, did the village fully divide into Muslim and Croat parts?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. During the day, people would still walk about freely; they were going to Vitez and other places. But at night, people would not cross the line.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You talked about the village guards. You said that the purpose of these guards was to protect the village from potential JNA attacks, and the criminal element had appeared in the area. Do you recall whether any of the men in your village was involved in late 1992 or earlier in going to the defence lines against the Serbs at Mount Vlasic?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Four or five young men went to Mount Vlasic, to Turbe, and also to Jajce.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You said that there were about four or five. After these men came back from their shift, would they still be involved in the guard duties?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you remember whether these men went to the shift at Mount Vlasic, Turbe, even in 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you remember whether it was these men, on the date when the general conflict broke out, on 16 April, that these were exactly the men who had been cut off in that area?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They were not home.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The other people who did not go to their shifts and were involved in the village guards, unlike those five who were on the front line, they went about their usual business.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. When they were not on guard duty, they were involved in their daily activities. They would go to the fields to work them and go to town.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Just one more question before the break, Mr. Krizanovic. You just described how your fellow villagers went to the shifts to fight the JNA. Did your Muslim neighbours also join this effort against the JNA?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. From what I know, they went to the front line at Visoko.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And this is the territory in the direction of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, perhaps this is a convenient moment to take a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Krizanovic, we are going to adjourn now for half an hour for a break. During the break, don't speak to anybody about your evidence until it's over; don't let anybody speak to you about it. That includes members of the Defence team. Would you be back, please, at half past eleven.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krizanovic, let us take up from where we stopped before the break. We have reached item 2.8 in your summary, that is, the date of the 16th of April, 1993. At that time, you had barely turned 18?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, on the 3rd of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Will you please, in your own words, and in a few sentences, tell us what you remember of that day?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: The 16th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, the 16th.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: In the evening of the 15th, I came back home from the town, naturally, being a young man I was out, and I went to bed, perhaps around 11.00 or half past. In the morning, I was wakened by gunfire, detonations, and my mother came. She was frightened. She did not know what it was about. So I woke up, went out, could hear gunfire from all sides because from where my village is, one can see a lot of ground around. So I came out. And there was my father's rifle. Since he was at work, that's the kind of job that he had, he had to do night shifts. So I stood by my house as my family was in my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Very well. Will you tell me if on that evening, on the 15th of April, you went out into Vitez like all the young men do, and met your friends there?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you observe something, some events or some mood which would perhaps be different from the usual?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, no, I didn't, because there were always troops around the town wearing camouflage uniforms, naturally, but everything was as usual. The discotheques were open, the coffee shops were open, and we were in a discotheque.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Very well. You told us that your father was working that night, he was at the SPS. But why did he have to be there? What was his job? Why did he have to work that night?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: He was involved with the water supply line there. Somebody had always to be on duty since they had water pumps there and, as far as I know, the Princip could not work without water, without steam.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your father, as a village guard, had a rifle, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Very well. So you told us that you heard gunfire from neighbouring villages, from directions. And in your village, at that time, when you awoke, was there any gunfire there? Was there any gunfire in the village proper?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And what did you do on the days that followed, that is on the 16th and then --

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, next to my house was my uncle's house, and of those families of the Bosniak. And we were at home. We were not really abreast of what was going on, so we were around our houses, would go into the house and eat, and then at night, we did not go to sleep. And that was that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So you didn't go away from your village?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Not to the village. I never went away from my home, from my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I see. You say that from -- in front of your house, one can see the surroundings, and what did you see on the 16th and the following days happen around you?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, for instance, across our village, Gacice, there's only Donje Veceriska, and one could hear -- see smoke and hear gunfire. Likewise Krcevine because opposite, on the other side, and the position is such that you could see. Ahmici could also be seen, that is, smoke, gunfire, but we could not really establish where the gunfire was coming from, because it came from all sides. And Mahalla was also near, about 700 or 800 metres as the crow flies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I suppose, since you said you could hear gunfire from all sides, that then you realised that something serious was going on? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that there was a war on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And you told us that, in point of fact, you remained in front of your house, that you never left the village and that your family was there.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us what you mean by family, your father, your mother?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: No, my father was at the Princip, I was working but there was my mother, there were my sisters, my uncle's wife, two children under age.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And when did the gunfire and the fighting begin in your village?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: On the 24th [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So that was four days after you woke up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: There is an error in the transcript, 20 April, not 24 April.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Will you tell us in a few words what do you remember of that first day of the conflict in the village, the 20th of April, what happened then?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: It was early in the morning. We heard the gunfire. There were -- well, say, about 25 of us in the village. We were not all armed. And we could hear the gunfire. I couldn't establish where it came from. But then lads from the neighbouring Mlakici came to lend us support and also from the village guards, because they were also down there, and that was a purely Croat village. There were no Muslims households there. So about 10 or 15 lads from Vitezovi came and about a dozen, about 10 members of the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: When you say you heard the gunfire, does that mean that the lower part of the village, where you were, was exposed to the gunfire from the upper part, or how was it?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: I couldn't really tell you because there was no gunfire around my house, and I cannot see the whole village because it's quite hilly, so you cannot really see well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You mentioned that your village guards were reinforced by men from the village of Mlakici, which is below your village. How far is it, roughly?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, about 500 or 600 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You also mentioned that to help you defend your village, some 15 lads from the Vitezovi unit came; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Before that gunfire, where were those lads stationed? I mean the Vitezovi.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: I think they must have been in Mlakici, because Mlakici is right next to Stari Vitez, to Mahala. But I don't know, I didn't see, because they arrived in no time at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Before that morning, the 20th of April, you did not see those lads from the Vitezovi.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You also said that about ten policemen from Vitez came.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Those policemen, I don't know who they were. Some of them had a patch saying "Police," but that was all, so I don't know which police it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Very well. You already mentioned that in your part of the village, that is, the part of the village that you lived in which had a Croat majority, there were about 20 village guards.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, thereabouts; 20 to 25.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the upper part of the village, which was predominantly Muslim? How many men there were members of the village guards at that time?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I should say around 80, because there were some refugees who were also able-bodied and who had brought weapons with them and uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So in addition to your neighbours, your villagers, you are telling us that there were people who came from outside.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So when one compares, when one juxtaposes these figures, in the lower part of the village, you were far outnumbered by the upper part of the village.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In terms of numbers, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What happened then? How long did the fighting last?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the fighting in the village, about seven, perhaps eight hours, there was gunfire.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What did you do during the fighting?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: I was at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And your father?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: He was at the Princip, he was at work. He couldn't come.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So you were at home, your mother, your relative, and the children.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You told us that the fighting went on for some eight hours. What happened then when it stopped, or rather how did it come to an end?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, there, around my house, the Muslims that were there, they surrendered. There wasn't any gunfire to speak of. They laid down their weapons, some 30, 25 of them, perhaps. Civilians were also removed and they were put in a garage while there was still gunfire above there. The civilians were also put in a house to avoid anything happening, you know, a stray bullet which perhaps might hit somebody.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So a number of your Muslim neighbours and refugees surrendered their weapons -- with their weapons. What about the rest?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, those Muslims in the upper part of the village, they were most able-bodied and they all fled. Because above the village there are no settlements, there's only forest, and at the same time one could go through there to Kruscica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What, then, happened to those civilians, to women and children who stayed back in the village? I mean women and children of Muslim ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: They were accommodated in houses; that is, they went back to their houses, and men were taken away.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Just to round this off. In the village and around the village, did anyone harass in any way or abuse those civilians, those women and children who had stayed and returned to their houses, any one of you, the villagers there?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: No. Even the women of those men who were put up somewhere - I don't know where - we even lent them vehicles or helped them to -- we drove them there to take food to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did UNPROFOR come to the village?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What did they do there?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: They brought some lunch packages; they brought the humanitarian relief.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You mentioned this group of men with weapons who had surrendered, that that group was taken away from the village.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Who took them away?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was the Vitezovi members.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know where they took them to?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know what then happened to those men who were taken away?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't. But I know that four or five days later, I don't know exactly, they returned to the village, they were brought back to the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Meanwhile, the hostilities were brought to an end in the area, or did the fighting go on?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: When the gunfire in the village stopped, we came out above the village and formed sort of a line next to the village, going by the Princip fence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
