utterances.text: Mr. Krizanovic, you told us that your father stayed at the SPS, at his job, during the fighting. When did he eventually manage to get back home?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was on the tenth or, perhaps, eleventh day of war. I don't remember exactly when the shift came. Because when the war broke out, all the communications were cut off, all the roads were cut off. And when his shift arrived, then he made it home.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So he had to work all the time at the SPS, did he?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What happened then? Could you tell us what happened in early July to your father?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: My father and my uncle, his brother, went to our field which is above the village to make hay for the cattle. Somebody was there and killed my father, and my uncle was wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What is your uncle's name?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Franjo Krizanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Franjo?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So at the time that they were mowing the grass, fire was opened on them.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Was there anyone else with them?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: You mean up there in another field? There were four young men, boys; two of them were underage. They were taken away. They were captured and taken to Kruscica, and they were kept there for about two months. Sometime in September they were released.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: But tell us, who captured them and took them to Kruscica?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: The BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Would you know who opened fire on your father and uncle?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: The army, I guess. Those boys who were taken were taken away by the army. It was all done very quick so that nobody could see them or hear them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you still remember who they were? Do you know the names of any one of those four that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Three were my relatives: Ivica Krizanovic, Nenad Krizanovic, Stipo Krizanovic. And Goran Strukar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You mentioned that two of them were underage; which ones of those four?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Nenad and Ivica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: How old were they?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Fifteen, sixteen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And they were taken to Kruscica, were they?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Which army formation at that time held the village of Kruscica?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: The BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to talk to one of those boys after their return to the village?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And what did they tell you about their stay in Kruscica?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, about Goran, and at least that is what he said, that he was not registered with the Red Cross, that he was taken to Zabrdze, that up there, he had to remove our mines, had to pull out their dead, and that he was told that he would be killed. And on the 28th of July, he managed to escape.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And the lot of those others, what did they have to do in Kruscica?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: They had to dig, that is at least what they told me. That they had to dig a hole for some plant because there is a river next to Kruscica. And they were there, they were in prison in the "black house". They were -- all their hair was shaved, and they were given some coveralls and their own clothes had been taken away. They had to dig trenches. They were brought to Kruscica to Fatina Vodica where the front line was and they talked, and that was that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You tell us that in Kruscica, they were detained in a structure called the "black house". Could you tell us if that -- that particular building was -- for some reason enjoyed some reputation in the village?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, before the war, it was kind of a monument because allegedly it had been an Ustasha camp during the World War II.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So the BH army, they detained those captured boys in the former Ustasha camp of the World War II?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: At that time, you had just come of age. So did you, at any time, join the Vitez Brigade, any of its units?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, listen, when the war broke out, I was 18 so I had to go. And I did not know what the name of the formation was. It was only in May or perhaps even June. I wouldn't know when we were given pieces of paper about 10 by 10 centimetres with my name and my particulars, and saying that I was a member of the 3rd Battalion, 3rd Company of the Vitez Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Who gave you that piece of paper with those particulars?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: My village commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And his name was?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Oh, come, I don't really know because they changed. I can't remember. It was a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And do you perhaps know, from who did this commander of the village guard get the particulars for those pieces of paper that he distributed?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Why, from us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You are telling us that it was sometime in May or June 1993.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Have you kept that piece of paper, perhaps, that you were given then?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: I think I do have it at home still to this day, that small piece of paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Would you mind putting it at our disposal?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't, only if I can find it at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And until when were you engaged with that military unit?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Until the 20th of June, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And after that, you did what?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: And then I went to the civilian police in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you have -- have you had an opportunity, for instance, of seeing some official document regulating your membership in the HVO, that is, an armed formation?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. When I was handing over my weapons and quitting the army, I had to sign a paper of discharge and to request a document showing that I was changing from the brigade to the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And what did that paper, what you had to sign, say? Since when had you been a member of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, what it said was 1992, in my case, April 1992. Even though in my military booklet, it says the 16th of April 1993 to the 16th of February 1994 is indicated as my military service.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: If I understand you well, the military document which you call the military booklet, and every man fit to serve the army in Bosnia-Herzegovina has, it indicates the 16th of April as the first day, and in some other documents, there is an earlier date indicated?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The military booklet calls it the military service.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: But in this other document, it says 1992 as participation in war?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. It must have been because of these certificates, the shares.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And have you earned the right to those shares, to those certificates?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And what have you done with them?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Nothing. I keep them at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can you use it to buy something?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Krizanovic. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: No questions, from Mr. Kordic's Defence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, one of the core documents that I will be referring to is a sealed document which was the signed witness testimony of Witness AP. In a fairly unusual move, the witness's testimony was permitted to be the direct. It was an agreement with the Defence. I just wanted to remind the Court of that. Any reference that I make to it -- what I think might be helpful, if the Defence agrees, is cite the paragraph number and then, without putting it on the ELMO, so to protect the integrity of the document and the witness' ID.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Mr. Krizanovic, as of the 16th of April, 1993, there was a general mobilisation order, was there not, for the HVO? Are you familiar with that?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your summary and your testimony based on 2.7, point 2.7, indicates that there were about five members of the Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I would ask the usher to present, please, Z653 to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What you have in front of you, Mr. Krizanovic, is a document of 14 April 1993 which lists -- which is a time after which the Vitez Brigade was officially on paper known as the Vitez Brigade. And at the very bottom of the page where it says 2nd Company, the last entry gives Gacice as the Vitez Brigade -- as part of the Vitez Brigade also having five Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. persons. Do you see that? Do you concur that that refers to your village?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you. There has been testimony in this Court, as I have just referred to, by a witness who has sought protection, but from your village to the effect that approximately September, 1992, and this -- excuse me -- yes, the exhibit -- Ms. Verhaag reminds me of the summary. His, under seal, is Z1771.2, summary of Witness AP. The second paragraph of that summary indicates that the witness saw weapons which included machine-guns taken by truck being stored behind the house of Croat neighbours, Zarko and Marko Krizanovic, and that the witness saw such weapons deliveries approximately three times per week. Can you explain, please, from where these weapons came and why you were having them stored at your residence?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Those weapons didn't come at all. What would we do with all these weapons?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Are you familiar with activity directed toward Muslim businesses in October 1992 in Vitez, principally in the town, but also throughout the municipality in which Muslim businesses or owners of Muslim businesses were harassed about the currency used for business transactions and then simply harassed because they were Muslims? Are you aware of that behaviour?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: I know that we went to get fuel at the petrol station at Krehic that I paid in marks. I don't remember. I don't know about this.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You indicated that relatives of yours were taken by units of the ABiH and you indicated one particular individual whose name I believe is Stipo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Stipo.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Are you able to indicate in what month or perhaps -- in what month was he taken and held?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Stipo Krizanovic was taken away on the 1st of July, 1993 from the village of Kladovo where my father was killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Please, if I may ask the usher to present Z1135.1.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: In front of you is a document that is a note by an officer of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the 3rd Corps, the 325th Mountain Brigade dated 2 July 1993, memorialising an interview with Stipo Krizanovic, son of Josip. Is Josip the name of Stipo Krizanovic's father?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And in this official note, as it is called, there is a discussion about the particular persons who attacked the Muslims at Gacice on the 20th of April --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, there's the usual objection. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm sorry that I have to interrupt my learned colleague, the Prosecutor, but it seems to me that this is a document which represents an official note of the BH army organs from 1993. Actually, this is a witness statement presented to the military police of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Of course we do oppose the introduction of this kind of document because it has the same kind of significance as the other documents that the Prosecutor wished to tender earlier on and that were refused through your decision.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. May I comment, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: This document will also be borne out. The point that I'm trying to make is a limited point, but the point will be borne out in paragraph 33 - the relevance of it I think is evident - of the document which is under seal, 1771.2.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I add, the only point I'm trying to make is an identification which is number 17, and that is the point that is borne out by Witness AP. Note the name, number 17, and nothing more from this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mikulicic, the Trial Chamber would seek further information as to what you declared, that is, that this document is to be rejected, because we have already decided in that way; we have rejected similar documents, you said. Could you to explain us further why? We didn't quite understand what you meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed, Your Honour. I simply didn't want to take up too much of your time. This document is a witness statement which was given to the military police of the BH army. It is not a signed witness statement. We do not know under which circumstances this statement was taken. We have not been given the right to cross-examine this witness. We do not know whether it was given voluntarily or whether the person was forced to do so. This has not been disclosed to us earlier; this is the first time we see it. Finally, may I say that the Defence of Mr. Cerkez and the Defence of Mr. Kordic were not allowed to use such documents during their cross-examinations respectively.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't recollect that ruling which prevented the use of documents being put to witnesses in order to test their credibility. What I have in mind is that the document, whether it should be admitted as an exhibit or not, should be allowed to be used by the Prosecution to test the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, I absolutely agree with that, that the Prosecutor should be allowed to test our witness. However, I do not agree that this test has to be carried out through a document whose authenticity is basically doubtful and which was not disclosed to the Defence in earlier proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, may I just ...

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The Judges' microphones are on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Judge May. May I just inform the Bench that Ms. Verhaag informed me that the Court has admitted a similar official note in the Novi Travnik; it is Exhibit 1963.12.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, I don't know that we can troll through all our earlier rulings. But, of course, we must maintain consistency. The Bench will admit this document since it clearly goes to the credit of the witness, contradicts what he said. But, of course, we bear in mind that questions of any weight, issues of authenticity - we'll notice what's said about it - those are matters which we will have to bear in mind in due course. But it's certainly admissible for the purpose of contradicting the witness, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Mr. Krizanovic, your direct testimony was that you were at home during the attack on the 20th. Your cousin has indicated that you, in fact, were one of the attackers, listing you as number 17 on the list of persons who participated in the attack. Would you be able, please, to discuss your real role that day, or are you maintaining a different version of the facts?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, look, you see here in this list that all the military-aged, able-bodied men who lived in Gacice are on this list. We even have young men here who were not even in Gacice on that day. It says it very nicely, that they went from house to house, and this statement could have been made by any Muslim from the village.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Without leaving this document, I would like to call the Court's attention to paragraph 33 of Z1771.2, where Witness AP specifically states that the HVO told the witness' group to go down to the village in a column. They guarded them on both sides. "One soldier who had a mask on was asked by another HVO soldier why he was masked, 'because the Muslims will all be dead soon anyway,' whereupon the soldier removed the mask from his head and the witness saw that it was the witness' neighbour, Goran Krizanovic." The witness also recognised the following HVO neighbours: Boro Krizanovic, Slavko Krizanovic, Marko Krizanovic, Zarko Krizanovic, Anto Krizanovic, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Do you think perhaps it is merely coincidental that a second person - one a Muslim; the first a Croat, your cousin - has identified you as an attacker that day? Are they lying?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you clarify this question for me, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Is what I have just read to you a lie, or is it the truth?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: A lie.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the ultimatum which was presented by the HVO to the Muslim community in Gacice on the 17th of April, 1993, which is mentioned in your cousin's statement but further borne out by a report of the ECMM, the European Monitoring Mission, in Z754?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If perhaps the usher would distribute it, it might be helpful.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Mr. Krizanovic, the document is in English because that is the language in which it was written. On the first page of that document, it is point 3. The document is dated 20 April 1993. Under "Ceasefire Violations: Unconfirmed." "Shelling between HVO HQ and the PTT building in Vitez. HVO is said to be putting an ultimatum on Gacice, and after that failed, HVO is said to have started attacking this village." Were you aware of the ultimatum given to the Muslims to hand in their arms, to which your cousin refers, and the failure or the refusal of the Muslims to act in accordance?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Who is Dr. Krizanovic?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Anto Krizanovic, nicknamed Doctor.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What was his role in the village of Gacice? Did he have an official position in the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Was he your relative?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And you did not know that he was a commander of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, no. I told you that this changed, that, in fact, we did not have a real commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your relationship to Mario Cerkez, how long have you known Mario Cerkez, or do you know him?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: I personally never saw Mr. Cerkez. I knew that he was commander of the Vitez Brigade, of course. But I had never seen him in my life.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The Vitez Brigade, are you familiar that that is the brigade from which the Stjepan Tomasevic -- into which the Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade grew? Do you know anything about the brigade structures in the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You have indicated that it was the Vitezovi, I believe, that perpetrated the attack on the village of Gacice. This is borne out in your cousin's interview, as well as other testimony. Do you know anything about the Vitezovi, who the commander was?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think, to be fair to the witness, he's not indicated that it was the Vitezovi who perpetrated the attack. That, of course, is your case.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I'm sorry. I was looking at 2.13 in his summary which specifically makes the reference.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Are you familiar with a group known as the Vitezovi?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Do you know who its leader was at the time of this incident in April 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Darko Kraljevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you personally know Darko Kraljevic?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Z651.3, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: In front of you is a document of 13 April 1993, which is signed -- comes out under the signature of a person named Ramljak and Damjanovic, operative duty officers of the Viteska Brigade. And it is a report concerning alleged attacks against the head of the Vitezovi whom you have identified as Darko Kraljevic, and other members. It appears from this document that "We," meaning apparently the Vitez Brigade, "took numerous actions after which they were released sometime around 1730 hours, about which you," having addressed this to the Central Bosnia Operative Zone in Vitez, will be informed. Did you know anything about this attack on Darko Kraljevic at this time, on this date, that is the subject of this report?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: I have never seen this document. I never had a chance to see this document. I don't know when this was. I can't remember. At that time I wasn't even interested in that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Well, it simply indicates that it was the area of responsibility of the Vitez Brigade, and I wondered if you might have seen this. Thank you very much. The Hotel Vitez, have you been there? Do you know what it is?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, after the war, at wedding parties.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You have never been to the Hotel Vitez prior to that?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Excuse me for just a minute. Let me get the paragraph. The soldiers identified by Witness AP in paragraph 36 took the group, containing Witness AP, to Vitez where at the time the BiH army was shelling the HVO headquarters at the Hotel Vitez. These civilians who were taken, these Muslim civilians, were essentially made human shields outside of that building, forbidden to enter for safety while the HVO members went in. Do you recall that incident? Do you recall taking a group of civilians down to the Hotel Vitez that day?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: I know that a group of civilians was taken and brought on the same day. Of course they lived in their homes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Do you know how many homes were left in the Muslim community after the attack on Gacice?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Houses were not left. Muslims still lived in houses, in houses that had remained undamaged, intact.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The -- again, turning to paragraph 36 of that same document, Witness AP confirms that, in fact, "The group was forced to go back to the seven Muslim houses which had not been burned. All 247 persons were forced to stay in these seven homes with no water for 16 days." Do you have any comment about only seven houses being left standing?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: They were without water? I was without water, and my family as well. Nobody had any water, electricity, nothing.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Returning for just a minute to your knowledge of Darko Kraljevic, the exhibit which was Defence Exhibit 89/2, if we could take a quick look at that, please. This is a report that was presented, it's actually a report by, I believe, Darko Kraljevic. And on the first page, there is a reference to 19 April, "The line on the Kuber elevation, Busovaca municipality, was won back." And the next entry is, "The village of Gacice was cleared." Would you have any comment or would you understand what might be meant by that in a report by the Vitezovi? Can you help us understand that?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: I only know that the 19th is the wrong date of the beginning of the conflict in Gacice. And I don't know about the rest because I was not with the Vitezovi.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Fair enough. Exhibit 887.1, please. While we're waiting for the exhibit, can you comment on the number of persons who died, the number of Muslims who died during that attack? Are you able to give us insight as to the numbers?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: That was not an attack, and I think it was about five or six. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: In front of you, 887.1, is a report by ECMM monitor Hank Morsink and there is a reference in the -- under number two, it would be the third full paragraph confirming that, "Victims in Gacice," misspelled as Gracice, "and Donja Veceriska appeared to have been buried properly and the relatives decided not to remove them." The team -- excuse me. "The team asked the commander of the HVO brigade Vitez about the incident of Gacice. All Muslim families seemed to be forced to leave the village." I'm reading just from the bottom of the paragraph, Your Honours. "All Muslim families seemed to be forced to leave the village at 3 May in the evening. They were brought with cattle trucks to Dubravica and were told to go to Zenica on foot. The brigade commander accused extremists for this incident." Can you comment on this, please?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: At that time, I was not at home. I was at the front line above the village near the SPS, and I heard that some have volunteered to go and that was -- that was made possible to them. They were bussed there and I don't know about the rest.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Was there any effort by the HVO to rebuild, immediately, the houses which had been burned down, as much as only seven houses for Muslims remained standing? Are you aware of any such effort?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: It wasn't only seven standing, there were more. But the houses were not repaired because there was no sense repairing them, there was constant shelling. And also nobody thought of repairing them during the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did anyone expect the Muslims actually to return and stay there? Did you expect that?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Do you know how many men were taken prisoner during that -- taken prisoner by the HVO during that incident at Gacice?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: About 25 to 30. And during the day, people were coming out of the woods and bringing their weapons with them and surrendering.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Z750, please. Z750 is a report, an operations report, of 20th April 1993 by the Vitez Brigade command to the Central Bosnia Operative Zone in Vitez. And the text which I am referring in the middle says, "The Gacice village is 100 per cent completed. 47 men were taken prisoner. Women and children were sent home." Are you familiar with this particular report?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: No. But I believe that I said that 25 to 30 surrendered and then additional people came out of the woods and surrendered. So this could be part of that overall number, and not everyone was captured.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your description of relations between the Muslim community and the Croat community in Gacice, you indicated there were tensions. I'd like to ask you for your comment on a matter reported in an ECMM report of -- in Z796. And we'll just take a very quick glance, it will be on page 7 of that report. I am referring -- it is in English, to a comment at the top, Gacice, with its grids, "In an area of ethnic hatred, BritBat found a village where there was still the ability to cooperate. It is a mixed village split with Muslims in the south, Croats in the north. The villagers and the HVO have apparently protected the Muslims from attack by external HVO elements ie, from Vitez. The village had been shelled over the last five days, presumably by the BiH. All male Muslims had left the village." And this is dated 27 April 1993. Was that an accurate characterisation of the relations between the Muslim and Croat communities in your -- from your point of view?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Not all Muslims left the village. People who had been taken away were -- had come back and lived in their own house. As for those who escaped to the woods and then I don't know to where else, to Kruscica, they were not around.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you or your family members offer any shelter or assistance to any Muslims that day, the 20th of April?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: No. I was thinking about -- I was concerned more with how to move my family away, how to protect them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Had you ever lived outside of Bosnia? Did you ever live overseas?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The destruction to the village and particularly to Muslim institutions and homes in Gacice was described by Witness AP in the witness' testimony. There was, in addition to the mosque having been destroyed and some graffiti having been written on, I believe, the youth centre indicating Za Dom Spremni, which are exhibited Your Honours, as part of the testimony, there was considerable looting. There was a report that you were seen, taking from a Muslim home, a tractor and a bulldozer. Did you do that?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: No. That is an outright lie.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Do you own a tractor and bulldozer now or did you at any time in 1993 up until today, from 1993 up until today?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Excuse me one minute. In which municipality do you reside today?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Are you still residing in the village of Gacice?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Gacice 44. That is the house number from before the war and it's the family home.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Can you tell us today how many Muslims are residing in Gacice, if you know the count?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: 99 per cent of the pre-war population.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And what are relations today?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: There are contacts, but not to the extent that we had contacts before the war. People look after their own interests.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Was there any reprimand, that you are aware of, given to any persons in your village in the military, the HVO, from Mario Cerkez, the commander of the Viteska Brigade, after the incidents? Are you aware of any reprimands or any type of disciplinary action that may have been taken or any inquiry into events that might have been taken by Mario Cerkez shall I say both in connection with the actual firing on the village, and in the removal of the civilian population? Anything at all?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: I am not aware of it. I only know that later, after everything calmed down in the village, some people were taken to some defence lines, let's say at Kuber, which were considered to be sort of punitive assignments.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: A quick look at Z1085.2, please. This document dated 20 June 1993 is signed by Mario Cerkez as commander of the Vitez Brigade. And although you indicated that as to Gacice, specifically, you are unaware of anything, did you ever hear of a general order acknowledging -- this document essentially acknowledges that there may have been expulsion of non-Croats. Was any word spread about this document to you or other persons living in your village at any time after the 20th of April, 1993, and actually after the 20th of June, excuse me, 1993? Are you aware of this document? It doesn't say to Gacice. It just is a general document.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: I've never seen this document before.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: No further questions, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krizanovic, just a few very short questions. In the beginning, my learned friend asked you, and at one point you said that before the war, you were -- you were going to the petrol station and you paid in German marks, you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what petrol station that was?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that that was Asim or Kasim Krehic's private gas station.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So the owner of this gas station is a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And he accepted German marks without any questions?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: When the Bosnian dinar was introduced that first morning, he was taking it. After that, he refused to take it anymore. I didn't have any myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So if I understood you correctly, Mr. Krehic, a Muslim by ethnic origin did not take Bosnian dinars but only German marks for his gas?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You were shown the document Z651.3 regarding Mr. Darko Kraljevic, which you knew nothing about. I'm going to ask you something else. A location called Jeline Vode is mentioned. Do you know about this?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Before the war I used to work in the forest with my father, so I knew the place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know nearest to which village is this Jeline Vode?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: That is above Kruscica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know, after the breakout of hostilities, and even before that, in the early part of 1993, who predominantly had control of Kruscica, which formation?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: ABiH.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You were also shown the document about the damage to the mosque in Gacice. Can you tell us, was there a mosque in Gacice?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So it couldn't have been damaged since it didn't exist there.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: We have pointed out several times that you just turned 18 around the time when these hostilities in 1993 had broken out. Did you at that time know anything about the bulldozer? Did you know how to operate it?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I'd never been near one, let alone would have known how to operate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: One last question. You said that sometime in May or June you became a member of the Vitez Brigade, and you mentioned that little piece of paper that made you one. As a soldier of the Vitez Brigade, did you ever receive any written orders from anyone?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, I was very young, and then I was just a regular soldier, so there was no need for any of that. I was in the trench, I looked ahead of me, and that was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So I assume that you just received orders from your immediate superior.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KRIZANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was from my sergeant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Krizanovic, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give it. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is not easy for me to say, but we are out of witnesses for this week and that is, I must apologise, due to the circumstances which were beyond our control. However, we did learn some lesson and we will simply put some reserve witnesses here on the side. I mean, we just didn't want to waste the time of the witnesses, the resources of the Court, et cetera. We were very conservative in our planning. From now on we will go a little bit more on the luxury side, I should say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, you should because this is the second week we've ran out of witnesses. We ran out in the week before the recess. Next week is a slightly shorter week than usual. But nonetheless, if you would plan for the rest of your case to have witnesses in reserve. It is inconvenient for them, but equally it is inconvenient for the Court not to sit, and it runs up expenses and it means that meeting the various deadlines that we've set is that much more difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, there is no need to confirm that. We are certainly -- I mean, we are learning the lessons and we are doing that. We'll do our best; that is all I can promise. Perhaps, Your Honour, while we are here, probably we can waste the time until lunch --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're not going to waste the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, spend for another purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Not more than usual.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. We are also considering having the accused, Mr. Mario Cerkez, testify at the end of our case. However, just as a matter of courtesy, we would like to inform the Court about that, that we are working on that, and it does need, certainly, time, time for the accused to see documents which were introduced in the case. As you are certainly aware, there are quite a lot of documents which were not seen during the testimonies, so not directly on the tables here; rather, they were introduced in files after the trial, and those are most of the documents which our client did not see. Those documents which are entered in live, if I may say so, during the trial day, are mostly shown to our client. However, we should go through those files in the prison. It is a matter of logistics and time, of course. We would ask the Chamber to consider allocating a couple of days to us, let's say four to five working days not counting the weekend, because the weekend is not available for the visitors in the detention unit - there are simply no conditions to work, and they refuse even to have the lawyers during the weekends - so we would ask sometime at the end of our case that some time is allocated to us. And I guess both counsel need it in order to concentrate the effort and go through the documents with the accused so that we really have effective testimony in the manner of asking questions about certain evidence. Of course, there is plenty of time to think about it and to see how we can do it. But we have been dealing with the idea of how to organise that work for quite a long time, and we simply don't see another option except having a couple of extra days allocated for that. Of course, I'm not asking for any additional time. I'm only asking that we are planning on the basis of staying within the time you defined in the calendar; that means before the 20th of October. We will also --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If it's necessary, providing the other evidence is being called, if it's necessary to take a day or two and it's reasonable, of course we would consider such an application.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, sir. In due time we will definitely ask for it, if required. Of course, I'm not entering into the details, but one of the aspects, just as a matter of information, is that it depends how many witnesses we can get, because certainly we also have a problem with the witnesses like the Prosecution did. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sayers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: One short matter, Mr. President. It's just really a matter of dotting the I's and crossing the T's. Our client has expressed a desire to see the testimony of General Petkovic and also Colonel Palavra in a language which he understands. We have the transcripts, obviously. We've made a request to the registrar. The registrar has consulted the orders and said that they don't have a problem in providing us with copies of the videotapes, but the orders only specifically release -- authorise release of the transcript. With the Court's permission, we would ask for the orders be enlarged to provide for the provision of the videotapes, videotaped testimony to us so our client can actually see it in a language which he understands, rather than having 500 or so pages translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is it an order of our Chamber or the order of another Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: It's the order of this Chamber, Your Honour. You've actually ordered the transcripts to be released to us. They had actually been.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we may join this request. When it is copied, it should be easier to copy two samples.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, I've got the order kindly provided by the registrar. The 5th of April. Yes, it will be enlarged to include the tapes. And we have, Mr. Sayers, while we're dealing with your case, a letter from you about your two affidavit witnesses who you want find.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: One is just in too poor health to testify and the other has declined to testify. It seems the Court's prior ruling excluding their affidavits stands. The third witness, Father Franjo Krizanac, is prepared to testify. As we pointed out, we have made arrangements for him to appear on the 26th of September, with the Court's permission, if that's acceptable for everybody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could just make a couple of points. I'm grateful to Mr. Kovacic for explaining the position about his evidence. I observe, I think, in fact, that we've got apart from Friday now free, we've got next Friday free on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We've got a Friday two weeks hence free and the Monday and Tuesday, I think, of the following week. If Mr. Cerkez is going to testify, obviously we'd be assisted by the earliest possible notice of any summary of evidence that he's going to give.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Are you entitled to a summary of his evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Whether there's a summary -- whether we're entitled to it or not, we'd like one. I think in the Rule, summaries are to be provided, generally, in any event. There's no reason why a summary shouldn't be provided, because the Cerkez evidence is likely to take some time, and there's no reason why it should be dealt with in any other way from any other witnesses. Which brings me back to next week's witnesses. As I understand it, it's three and a half days next week. There's a half a day off and no Friday at all, so I think it's three and a half days altogether. I think there's a half day --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There's a Plenary meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It may only be a quarter of the day. There are present listed nine witnesses. The last one, the ninth, is one of those who's been added, apparently. We have no summary of any kind in respect of that witness. So I can't even start to prepare for her. I would -- it's going to be quite a task to prepare for eight or nine witnesses and to dispose of them in three and a half days. The best method of abbreviating cross-examination is to have, of course, the most early notice of the detail of what's going to be said, or assuming I then have the resources to deal with it. I'm asking Mr. Kovacic if he's able to provide us summaries in draft form of any of the witnesses at an early date, to do so, because it will make our life that much more easy and it will make it much more possible for us to prepare properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: One other thing that I'm reminded that I should have said, though I don't want to wreck my learned friends' weekends in any way, but if they want to work at the weekends, it may be that the Chamber would be able to achieve for them by its order or request that which they can't achieve directly. Because I can see that the pressures of time for us to finish by Christmas are, in fact, great and getting greater. I know more things about my position than are presently revealed, and I think that the pressures are going to increase.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, therefore, we must do all that we can to achieve the objective. Mr. Kovacic, it is right that there are several days available. Next week there's a day and a half, and there are other days. It may be that you're travelling during some of that time, but there will be time available during the trial. As for next week, we will do our best to get through what we can. I will explore the possibility of sitting slightly longer hours, if necessary, to try and get through your witnesses in the short time. Of course, it assists if the summaries could be available as promptly as can be. We'll also look to see if you can get into the detention centre during the weekends, if it's an emergency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: We are appreciating this, sir, very much. Just also for understanding the situation, our client is also receiving from time to time family visits, and we are of course giving priority to that, as is the case for next week, for example. So unfortunately, we wouldn't bother the client in that occasion. Yes, we are counting on that, that we will use all the available time, if some appears during the trial. But if I may just in two sentences answer my dear colleague. We did supply all the summaries required by the Court order, short summaries for the purpose of the trial. We transmitted all of those witnesses, some of them were transmitted additionally, in later phase, but we did transmit it. So far, I understand my dear colleague, in our daily communication, that they are quite satisfied with the time when we are transmitting the summaries we are using here in the trial. We are doing our best, and I will warn -- I will notice also the other side that, for example, our witnesses for next week will be coming Friday evening in The Hague. So we are starting to prepare the summaries we are using here on the trial, we will start to work on that on Saturday morning. We cannot do it, physically, any other time. So we are working through Saturday and Sunday and we are delivering as soon as it is done, so probably one or two on Saturday, one or two on Sunday. In addition, we are going beyond our obligation, I can claim that. For example, last weekend, unfortunately the fax machine of the Prosecution office was out of order, and we were ready to deliver one on Saturday, one on Sunday -- I guess, two on Sunday, I don't remember exactly. But then I delivered personally, in the envelope and left down on the reception desk, so we are doing more than required. And I would remind the Chamber that we received summaries very often a hot copy, in the morning, in the moment we entered this courtroom. So those are not summaries that somebody is preparing a cross-examination. The other materials earlier entered in the case is, but I will, of course, do my best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll sit, as far as the trial is concerned, next on Monday morning at half past 9.00. Let's have a word with the legal officer, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
